items.body: China And St. Augustine - Gavekal Research China And St. Augustine Louis-Vincent Gave Gavekal Research | 23 Oct 2026 Back in the summer of 2015, the Chinese government decided that equity markets had risen too far, too fast. The rug was pulled from under margin lending and various restrictions were put in place that brought the unfolding raging equity bull market to an abrupt end. By January 2024, the Chinese government reversed course and decided that Chinese equity prices had fallen far enough. Beijing intervened in the market (see Chinese Policies And Chinese Equities ) and put a floor under domestic markets. Equities duly rallied, delivering very solid returns for 2024 and 2025. However, over the past year, Chinese equity market returns have been fairly dismal. In fact, Chinese equity markets have now fallen for 10 consecutive weeks, a feat they had never achieved before. This in spite of the fact that (a) excitement over all things “artificial intelligence” has been a key driver of global equity market performance and that (b) China is one of the few countries outside of the US actually registering notable gains on the AI front. In short, Chinese equities have had a very disappointing month, quarter, year-to-date and 12 months and what had been steady outperformance has now melted away like snow in the sun. items.body: Musings on Markets: From Eyeballs to Annual Run Rates (ARR): Buzzy Pricing Metrics and the Anthropic Trade! Thursday, October 22, 2026 From Eyeballs to Annual Run Rates (ARR): Buzzy Pricing Metrics and the Anthropic Trade! I was in San Francisco last week to talk to NYU Stern Alumni on October 15, and it was the day that Anthropic had a pre-IPO meeting with prospective investors. While I was not at the meeting, the focus of teh gathering was laying a foundation for its upcoming IPO, with the company reporting third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion, which news reports described as surging 45% over the previous quarter's revenues, and positive profits, albeit on an adjusted basis. During the meeting, Anthropic also reported an annual revenue run rate (ARR) of $67 billion, a metric that those in the AI space have adopted with gusto, with an estimate that the ARR would exceed $100 billion by the end of the year. The nature of ARR, where choices on how revenue is calculated (gross versus net) and on annualization periods (daily, weekly or monthly) can make a significant difference, has led investors to be skeptical about comparing these numbers across time and companies. While I share some of that skepticism, it is worth remembering that young businesses are often priced on inventive metrics, some with more basis than others. In the late nineties, dot.com companies were priced not just on the number of visitors to their websites, but on eyeballs , where Mary Meeker argued that ad spending at these companies was correlated with time that these visitors spent on websites (eyeballs), rather than with total visitors. In the last decade, you saw social media companies priced based upon the number of users and subscription-based companies on subscriber numbers. In this post, I will try to lay out the rationale for why pricing supplants valuation in young companies and why that pricing almost always has to be built around messy metrics like eyeballs, users and ARR, rather than more conventional metrics like earnings, book value or cash flows. Young Companies in a Corporate Life Cycle All businesses, no matter how large and established they might be today, started as young businesses and matured. With that perspective in mind, I will start this discussion by placing young businesses in a corporate life cycle in the figure below: One of the first steps in analyzing a company is placing it in the right stage of the life cycle, and there are three choices that you can use in making this placement: Chronological age : The first and simplest choice is to look at the age of a business, putting companies that have been in operation for short periods into the young company grouping and classifying those that have been in operation for longer as mature. While this approach is easy to use, and for the most part, effective, it can be misleading in businesses like infrastructure, where it can take decades to get established, and in technology, where the lack of capital intensity can allow a company can go from start-up to mature in a few years. Industry grouping : Another choice is categorizing industry groups into life cycle stages and assuming that any company that belongs to a specific industry group shares its life cycle characteristics. For decades, investors have viewed technology as a shorthand for growth and put technology companies into the earlier stages of the life cycle and utilities as mature or even declining and put all utility companies into the mature to declining company grouping. The limitation of this approach is that there will be divergence within each group, where some companies separate themselves from their industry group; there are mature and even declining companies that are in the technology grouping, and there are power companies that have taken advantage of the data center boom to become growth companies. With technology in particular, where companies age in dog years, I talked about how companies can get mis-categorized and sometimes mismanaged as growth companies , even though their best days are behind them. Operating metrics : Ultimately, life cycle effects show up in the operating metrics of companies, and there are common characteristics that young companies share, and they include the following: High revenue growth : Young companies usually have high revenue growth, and while this is usually off a small revenue base, there are exceptions, where companies with scaled up revenues are still able to show high growth. Operating losses : As young companies scale up, they usually struggle with unformed business models, and at low scale, their fixed costs overwhelm their revenues, resulting in negative or very low operating profit margins. Negative free cash flows : Free cash flows are after reinvestment, and as young companies invest to deliver on their potential growth, that reinvestment will generate negative free cash flows. Failure risk : The confluence of small revenues, losses and negative free cashflows, which must be funded with external capital (equity or debt) exposes young firms to significant risk of failure. The figure below captures the shifts in operating metrics, as companies move through the life cycle: Put simply, if a company has revenue growth in single digits, stable margins and positive free cash flows to the firm, it is a mature company, no matter how it views itself. Conversely, a firm with high revenue growth, negative or very low profit margins and large negative free cashflows to the firms is a young growth firm, no matter what its scale. Recognizing those characteristics is critical in understanding why so many give up on valuing young companies, and why pricing will often be based on unfamiliar metrics. How do Anthropic and OpenAI measure up in the life cycle? Using a patchwork of public data and leaked information, here are the numbers on key operating metrics that I have as of October 2026 for both companies: The sky-high revenue growth and operating losses are a clear indication that these are young, growth companies, but note that the revenues (albeit on an ARR basis) at both companies are already large, suggesting that they are growing at scale. That should come as no surprise, since they are both rumored to be looking at IPOs in excess of a trillion dollars, in terms of total market capitalization. The business models are still in flux in both companies, as they wrestle with how best to structure their business models (usage versus subscription) and struggle with market targeting questions (premium versus mass market). I know that Anthropic claimed to be profitable in the second quarter of 2026, but I don't think that even Anthropic believes this to be true, since these are adjusted profits and the adjustments represent a patchwork of add-backs of legitimate expenses. As for cash flows, both Anthropic and OpenAI are deep in the hole, with negative free cash flows, at the moment, and whether they are able to generate positive cash flows in the future is entirely a function of how the AI business evolves over time. Pricing versus Valuation: Across the life cycle I will start with a distinction that I believe needs to be made between two approaches to attaching numbers to assets and businesses. The first is to value that asset or business, based on its capacity to generate and grow cash flows, and the risk in those cashflows, i.e., intrinsic valuation. The second is to price that asset or business by looking at what others are paying for "similar' assets, thus reducing pricing to demand and supply. The picture below captures that difference: It is true that if you believed in efficient markets, price would converge on value, but if you did, you would save yourself the time and aggravation associated with trying to price or value assets by investing in index funds, and moving on to more productive pursuits. If you don't believe in efficient markets, you can take one of two paths. You can take the investor route , trying to value assets and businesses, with the intent of buying undervalued and/or selling overvalued companies, and hoping that price converges on value. Alternatively, you can take the trading path , where you throw up your hands on intrinsic value, arguing that it is too subjective and difficult to estimate, and make your money by buying investments at low prices and selling them at higher prices, using whatever tools (including charts and technical indicators) you want to use, to make your judgments. While you can value and price any business, there are reasons why the usage of each can vary depending upon where a company is in the life cycle. To value a business, you have to estimate expected future cash flows, and to make these estimates of cash flows, growth and risk, and you generally draw on three sources of information: Financial statements : The current financial statements of a company provide information on unit economics, profitability and risk, and historical financial statements are useful in assessing growth in the business and changes in business profitability. For mature businesses that have been in operating for long period, much or even all of what you need to value the company can be in its financial statements, but for younger companies, the current financials may not yield much (as growth and unformed business models create noise) and there is little history, Market size and growth : Knowing the size of the total market that a company is aiming for, and how quickly it is growing can help put reasonability constraints on the growth rate and market you estimate for a company. For companies in established markets, this should be relatively easy to do, but for companies in new and evolving markets, this can become difficult. Industry statistics : As you forecast profit margins and the risk profile for a company, having that information for the crosssection of companies in the industry can establish bounds and help in making estimates. If you frame an intrinsic valuation in terms of the big estimation questions that need to be addressed to arrive at value, starting with the cash flows from existing investments, moving on to estimating the value that will be added by future growth and assessing risk, you can see that valuing young companies will always be more complicated than valuing more mature businesses. In fact, looking at Anthropic and OpenAI, you can see why valuation will be daunting: While I am a glutton for punishment, and I will try, albeit with error, to make my best judgments on Anthropic's future cash flows, risk and value (as I did with SpaceX), when the prospectus is made public, I understand why most will turn away in the face of uncertainty and choose not to value the company. Some of these investors will also look at how those that they believe know more about that companies are assessing its value, and peruse prior venture capital rounds at both Anthropic and OpenAI for clues on value. Both Anthropic and OpenAI have been active in raising equity as private companies, and the most recent rounds yield estimates of what these private investors thought they were worth, at least at the time the capital was raised. The table below summarizes the number of VC rounds, with capital raised, at both companies, as well as the pricing in their most recent rounds: Anthropic's VC round in May 2026 , from a cross section of big-name venture capitalists, raised $65 billion for the company, at a post-money pricing of $965 billion . OpenAI's most recent capital raise was in March 2026, when it raised $122 billion, at a post-money pricing for the company at $852 billion . OpenAI also has a pending round of capital raise ahead of an IPO, where they expect to raise $30 billion with a pricing for the company of roughly $1.4 trillion . While you may be tempted to assume that the VC pricing in these rounds are rooted in value, venture capitalists are in the pricing game, as I have argued in prior posts , In fact, they, stretch pricing metrics and definitions of peer groups, and VC valuation is almost always forward pricing : In the case of Anthropic and OpenAI, this forward pricing process is both more compressed and even less informative than at most young companies, with investors viewing the companies as imminent IPOs, and pricing them based upon their expectations of the pricing of the public offering, and discounting that expected price for negative surprises about the company's prospects that may lower the pricing or delay/cancel the IPO: The expected pricing will be a function of pricing in prior VC rounds, management wishlists and even rumors, and the discount applied will increase as the time to the IPO lengthens and with the uncertainties about the company and its potential market. For Anthropic, for instance, at the time of the VC round, the expected pricing for the IPO was $1.15 trillion, well below what the expectations are today, and reflective of how much can change over short periods with young companies, and the $965 billion pricing in the VC round would have represented a $150 billion discount on the estimate. Pricing Process While the reluctance to value young companies, and fall back to pricing is understandable, I would push back on the notion that doing so dispenses with the need to make the assumptions about cashflows, growth and risk that are required in intrinsic valuation. In this section, I will break down the pricing process into steps, and look at the issues that you faced when valuing these companies also create impediments in pricing, and in the next section, why using a multiple of annualized revenue run rates (ARR) or even eyeballs makes implicit assumptions about future profitability, growth and reinvestment. The Steps in the Process If, in pricing, you attach a number to an asset or business, based upon what others are paying for similar assets or business, how exactly does this process play out when valuing a company or business? No matter who does the pricing, and how sophisticated they claim to be, there are three steps in pricing companies: Standardize the price : The nature of pricing shares in public markets is that the share price is a function of share count, which is arbitrary; a stock split for instance halves the price while doubling the count and total market capitalization or value is a function of company size. To allow for comparisons across companies, you standardize the market price by dividing by a common variable that you can obtain for each of the companies in your comparison, with the choices ranging from revenues (or revenue drivers) to earnings to cashflow variants to book value. Since the market price can be for just equity (market capitalization) or for the entire business (enterprise value, which includes net debt), the denominator has to be defined in the same terms, with equity (operating) income and book value of equity (invested capital) going with market capitalization (enterprise value). Find peer group companies : For pricing to be functional, you have to find other priced companies just like the one that you are pricing. The simplistic solution is to start with other companies in the same industry or business grouping, with added constraints on geography and company size thrown in. Needless to say, even if done with care, the choice of companies in the peer group is subjective and can vary across analysts and investors, even when looking at the same company. Control for differences : No mater what pricing metric (PE, EV to Sales etc.) you pick, there will be fundamental reasons why companies will trade at different values, and for a pricing to have substance, you have to control for differences. Thus, if PE ratio is your metric, a company that expects higher growth in earnings or lower risk than its peer group, should trade at a higher PE ratio than the peer group does, and that difference has to enter your discussion. The picture below captures these steps, with the variants on pricing metrics and the considerations in peer group construction included: While this process remains the same for every pricing, there are reasons why pricing metrics will vary across companies and why peer group construction may be easier in some cases than other, and I will take Anthropic and OpenAI through the process. 1. Pricing metrics With some companies, your choice of pricing metrics will span the spectrum, with revenues, earnings, cash flows and book value all competing as scalars. However, your choices will narrow at others, and one reason that is relevant to the Anthropic/OpenAI discussion is where a company falls in the life cycle: As you can see, early in the life cycle, when companies are losing money, have negative free cashflows and little tangible capital invested in assets in place, you will see revenue often as the only viable metric, leading to revenue multiples dominating the discourse. Put simply, desperation drives you up the income statement until you find a positive number. It should be no surprise, therefore, that the metric that companies and investors have focused on with Anthropic and OpenAI is revenues . Those revenues are growing so quickly at these companies, that their argument is that trailing numbers are dated by the time hey are released, and that has led to the shift to annualized revenue run rates (where using revenues from the last week or month allows for more updated vales). As we noted earlier, the perils with annualized revenue rates (ARR) is that they are not standardized and can be easily gamed. Just in the last few weeks, there have been news stories on the divergence between gross and net revenues with OpenAI shifting towards using the latter, lowering ARR from $70 billion to $50 billion, while Anthropic continues to report gross revenues and the cloud provider payments as expenses. In addition, you can compute ARR using the last day's, the last week's and the last month's revenues, and while Anthropic and OpenAI have both converged on monthly annualization, there is nothing that binds them to continue to do so. There is a second choice that will come into play as the debate about Anthropic's pricing becomes more heated, and that is whether to use revenues in a future period, i.e.. forward revenue . By forecasting the annualized revenue run rate of $100 billion plus by the end of 2026, Anthropic has already opened the door, but do not be surprised if investors and analysts shift to looking at revenues in 2030 or 2036, since scaling prices today to forward revenues five or ten years out will make the pricing multiple look lower, and thus more defensible. Once you decide to go forward in time, it is plausible that you can even shift to expected earnings in 2031 or 2036, built around expected operating or net profit margins; arguing that Anthropic is cheap because it trades (today) at 25 times 2036 earnings (based on your estimated revenues and net margins) brings the multiple back to earth, but at what cost? Investors use frames of what comprises normal or high, based upon their acquaintance with a multiple, and many will (mistakenly) compare these forwards earnings multiples to current earnings multiples in the market to make their investment judgment on cheap or expensive. There is a third choice, and that is to relate the pricing of these companies to a variable that you believe will be correlated with future revenues and earnings. With that choice, you can see the rationale for estimating enterprise value per user or subscriber for user and subscriber based companies, with the connector being the logic that more users and subscribers today is a leading indicator of higher revenues and earnings in the future. It was that logic that led Mary Meeker and other internet analysts to use website visitors and eyeballs in pricing dot com companies, and while you may disagree, the logic holds. With OpenAI and Anthropic, where the power, reach and revenues of AI agents is dependent on having access to compute power, you could scale the market cap and enterprise value at these companies to the compute power at each company, based upon either measures of compute power (in gigawatts) or money spent to acquire the power (compute commitments). The downside of using metrics that are specific to a business (users, eyeballs or compute power) is that you can compute that multiple only for the companies in this business, restricting comparisons, and you have no perspective on what comprises high, low or typical for that multiple. The table below captures the pricing metrics that emerge with each of these choices for Anthropic and OpenAI, at $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion dollar market capitalizations: As you can see, you can make the case that Anthropic is cheaper than OpenAI, based upon the most recent ARR or the ARR in 2026, but OpenAI is cheaper relative to expected revenues in 2030, compute costs/capacity and based on user count. Each of these pricing multiples comes with caveats, with obvious explanations for differences, some in how the metric is computed (gross revenues for Anthropic versus net revenues for OpenAI) and some in fundamentals (Anthropic is priced more highly more user, but given that its usage base is more enterprises than individuals, and that they pay based on usage, each Anthropic customer should be priced more highly than an OpenAI customer). No matter which of these pricing metrics you use, though, the truth is that it is entirely possible that both Anthropic and OpenAI may be overpriced, and by comparing the two, you are just finding the less overpriced entity. 2. The Peer Group challenge Pricing loses much of its power, without access to a peer group of similar companies that are priced in the market place. With a software, chemical or retail company, pricing becomes easier because you have dozens, or even hundreds, of companies that you can define as being in your peer group. It is true that the company you may be pricing may be an outlier in terms of growth and risk in your peer group, but that is a problem for the next section, where you have to control for differences. Pricing becomes much more difficult, when you have unique companies or companies in cutting edge businesses, where there are a handful or even no other companies that are comparable, with market pricing. Using both of these components (number of companies in the same space and whether they are publicly traded), there are four scenarios that play out, ranging from least to most difficult. If you are pricing a company in a business, where there are lots of publicly traded companies , you will not only have a choice of pricing multiples, but also more robust pricing, since each of the companies has an updated market price and the financial statements are standardized (GAAP or IFRS). If you are pricing a company in a business, where there are only a few publicly traded players , you may have a choice of multiples, but small sample size will reduce the power of your pricing, though having a long historical pricing record for all of the companies may sometimes compensate. For much of the last century, in the United States, GM and Ford were priced against each other, with traders developing ranges of what each company should trade at relative to the other. If you are pricing a company in a business, where there lots of companies that are privately held, as is often the case when you have a nascent business with lots of potential, you are confronting a challenge that many venture capitalists face, and you can try to get the most recent pricing for each company, though that pricing will often be dated (depending on when the last capital raise was) and sometimes untrustworthy. Your most difficult challenge will be when you are pricing a company in a business, where you have both very few companies in the space, and almost none are publicly traded. If you define peer group for Anthropic and OpenAI as other companies in the LLM space, you are in effect in the last category, since neither of the companies is traded yet, and their competitors are either parts of bigger businesses - Gemini is a small part of Alphabet, xAI is a bigger part of SpaceX which has other functioning and profitable businesses and Muse is obscured by Meta's advertising business. When Anthropic's IPO show hits the road, the lack of a peer group will be an impediment, but investors and traders are creative and come up with solutions: In the narrowest version of the pricing game , Anthropic and OpenAI will be twinned with each other, since they are not just competitors but also playing the same business game. Initially, or at least until OpenAI files its prospectus and goes public, the comparison will be between a public pricing for Anthropic and private pricing for OpenAI, with SpaceX thrown into the mix as a noisy peer. in a broader version of the pricing game , and especially if Anthropic is even close to its $1.5 trillion market cap, the comparisons will be to the Mag Seven companies, all of which command market capitalizations close to or well in excess of a trillion. The argument will be that investors who seek out large market cap companies will compare them to each other, even though Tesla, Apple and Anthropic are very different companies in terms of business model and where they are in the corporate life cycle. You could also bring in SpaceX, not part of the Mag Seven, but also a trillion dollar company perhaps at about the same stage of the life cycle: The table below compares Anthropic's pricing (using a target pricing of $1.5 and $ 2 trillion) to the pricing of the Mag Seven companies, as well as SpaceX: As with the pricing comparison with OpenAI, there is good news and bad news for Anthropic bulls and bears. The bulls can argue that Anthropic is cheaper than SpaceX, and that if it looks expensive relative to the Mag Seven, it is because it has higher expected growth. The bears will push back, noting that the AI buzz that is carrying Anthropic is also pushing SpaceX to highs, and that the yawning gap between the Mag Seven companies and Anthropic on revenues and earnings (which are not reported in this table, but make the case for the Mag Seven stronger) cannot be explained away with hope and potential. 3. The Connection to Value You can price a company based upon any metric that you choose to use, but if pressed on which metric is the best one, I will deflect (and perhaps deliver a non-response), because I don't believe that there is a "best" metric for pricing. The key, though, is that no matter what metric you pick, you should think through how that metric will play out in the company's value and what you need to control for in your pricing. Let's start simple with PE ratios and look at the chain that connects current earnings to overall value: The first link is earnings growth , to generate future earnings, with higher growth leading to higher value. The second is the efficiency with which you deliver that growth , which results in reinvestment, and converts earnings to growth; a company that can earn a higher return on equity on its reinvestment should be able to generate more in cash flows, for the same earnings, than a company that earns a lower return on equity. Finally, risk comes into play when you estimate the present value of future cash flows; less risky cash flows will allow you to use a lower discount rate and attach a higher value for equity. Put simply, when comparing PE ratios across companies, you have to control for differences in earnings growth, return on equity and equity risk. Since PE ratios are a non-starter with Anthropic and OpenAI, I will turn to enterprise value to revenues (using either the ARR or the trailing 12 month revenues): As you can see, for Anthropic to be highly priced relative to revenue, its revenues will have to not only grow a lot, but do so quickly , making the revenue growth rate and the speed at which it ramps up the first determinant of pricing. The second component is profitability , since the company is reporting sizable losses now, and can expect to do so in the near term, the "adjusted" profit kabuki dance notwithstanding. Here, there are two key determinants that will drive value, with the first being unit economics , since having higher gross margins will ease the pathway from losses to profits, and the second being economies of scale , with compute costs in particular growing slower than revenues, pushing up operating margins. The third is risk , with operating risk (from evolving business models), financial risk (from the compute commitments) and regulatory risk (from restrictions on AI) all coming into play; companies that are less exposed to these risks should be worth more. To make a case for Anthropic at a $1.5 or $2 trillion pricing, you will have to make defensible arguments for sky-high revenue growth in the early year, a surge in operating margins to 30% or higher, with favorable unit economics and economies of scale providing tailwinds and a risk profile that quickly converges towards the average, as regulatory risks recede and the business model finds it feet . While you may find this story to be a reach, it is a plausible one, and I plan to give those who tell the story a chance to make an argument, rather than dismissing it outright. Conclusion As Anthropic heads towards its initial public offering, my suggestion is that you step back from the frenzy, since like the parable of the six blind men who visit an elephant, and having touched different parts of it, come away with wildly different descriptions of what an elephant looks like, there will be Anthropic bulls and bears who will latch on to a part of the company's lore and spin tales about its future. Thus, an Anthropic bull whose entire argument for why you should buy the company is that it has had high revenue growth in the last year or that gross margins right now are 80% is telling part of a story, and not a very persuasive one, whereas a bear whose entire thesis is built around the company losing money and having negative cash flows is missing the narrative train just as badly. A full (bullish) story for Anthropic will be anchored in a belief that AI's reach in terms of market will give it a massive addressable market, that Anthropic will be one of the big winners in that market and that it will find a way to convert its dominance into market share and high profits; the high pricing will be justified with high revenue growth and great unit economics (with high gross margins) arguments. For bears, a fully thought through story will be premised on an AI market that struggles to get off the ground, partly because of flaws in AI agents, partly because of competition from cheaper open-source models and partly because of regulatory constraints, and Anthropic, as a company, is constrained by weak corporate governance and an untrustworthy management. The overpricing argument will point to the revenue growth that will be lower than anticipated, which combined with their compute commitments will lead to profit margin compression, will leave you at a much lower justified pricing. I will not be taking sides here, but not because I am copping out. It is because I am investor at heart and feel more comfortable making my decision based upon an intrinsic valuation of Anthropic, which will have to wait until the full prospectus gets filed (hopefully next week). items.body: Council on Foreign Relations Articles By experts and staff Updated October 11, 2026 12:00 a.m. Brad W. Setser CFR Expert Whitney Shepardson Senior Fellow There is an argument—made in the recent Geneva Report and by various former IMF officials —that China’s current export surge is the simple consequence of the housing downturn and the resulting weakness in Chinese internal demand.* The weakness in the RMB in this story is entirely incidental to the increase in exports, which is, more or less, a mechanical response to weak internal demand. Cannot sell excavators at home? Export them. Built more modern car capacity than your internal market supports ? Export that too… The fall in the nominal RMB over the course of 2022 and the first half of 2023 in nominal and read terms was simply a function of domestic macroeconomic weakness, and a growing rate differential. It wasn’t an active policy choice by China’s central bank. Now, some might note that China’s currency doesn’t always move with rate differentials. The RMB didn’t consistently get pulled up when Chinese rates were higher than U.S. rates (2002-2020 generally speaking), and while it did fall when rate differentials moved against the RMB in 2022 and 2023, it then stabilized and has even appreciated modestly since the middle of last year. That appreciation hasn’t been big enough to correct the deep undervaluation of the RMB, but it came at a time when the PBOC policy rate (the reverse repo rate) was well below the U.S. policy rate. China doesn’t have an open financial account. As a result, equilibrium in the foreign exchange market is thus driven far more by exporter conversion and current account flows than by rate differentials and financial flows.** That, together with China’s ongoing management of the exchange rate and a trade surplus that can generate significant inflows, means that the value of the RMB is much more of a policy variable under the independent control of the Chinese authorities than a simple byproduct of monetary and fiscal policies. The modern IMF is reluctant to accept this conclusion. Its surveillance has generally ignored China’s currency management (even if that management is relatively obvious; see the data on FX settlement) and its recent comprehensive assessment of China’s economy completely ignored the balance of payments and exchange rate management. But it is pretty obvious to the market, even if the PBOC , rather absurdly , insists that “market forces play a decisive role in determining the RMB exchange rate.” I doubt the PBOC can win this argument. I agree with Mark Sobel : “The renminbi is still heavily managed and the authorities have acted to slow appreciation. The paper states that the PBoC phased out ‘regular’ foreign exchange intervention in 2017. But it has many means at its disposal to achieve the same effect through extensive capital controls, administrative guidance, signalling at the fix and deploying state-owned commercial banks. These means are heavily used. Thus, the word ‘regular’ must be taken with a pinch of salt . The comparison to Japan, which intervenes occasionally, is spurious – the yen largely floats freely in integrated global markets. The same cannot be said for the renminbi.” In reality, the PBOC’s daily fix now plays the decisive role in the currency’s path, and the market is often a bet on how the PBOC’s management of the yuan will evolve. That is clear from the lack of volatility in the yuan’s rate against the dollar. The yuan’s move down against the dollar in 2022 was a controlled 10 percent move, and the appreciation over the last 16 months has been even more controlled crawl. And the market is clearly massaged with substantial help from the state banks. In fact that the pattern of changes in the monthly FX settlement data looks exactly like the pattern of intervention of a central bank managing its currency around a tight band (the state banks in practice buy FX to keep the CNY from testing the strong side of the band, so there is an asymmetry in how the CNY is managed). None of this would matter much if China’s economy was small. But that obviously isn’t the case. Nor would this matter much if China’s exports didn’t respond to changes in the RMB’s real (and nominal) value. But that is also not the case. There is abundant evidence that China’s exports do respond to moves in the currency. Periods of RMB weakness have consistently been associated with periods of especially rapid Chinese export growth. Chancellor Merz and President Macron got this right, even if macroeconomic issues haven’t yet figured prominently in the EU’s dialogue with China.*** As they note in their open letter to the European Commission : “An appreciation of undervalued currencies towards a value more in line with fundamentals would help support the rebalancing of trade accounts with the EU in the short and medium term … European policy discussions focused on forging a common understanding of these exchange rate issues and their interaction with global imbalances would be useful.” The best evidence that exports responded to changes in the currency, and not simply to changes in the path of China’s internal demand, is the acceleration in China’s export growth after the RMB’s depreciation over the course of 2022. This is the killer chart. Now, you might ask: what of the acceleration in export growth in 2020 and 2021? That was pretty clearly tied to the global increase in goods demand that came with the pandemic and work from home requirements. It was expected to fade when the world economy normalized. But it didn’t. By 2023 Chinese export growth again topped global trade growth. The general expectation that the rise in China’s goods surplus during Covid would prove to be “transitory” heavily influenced the IMF’s work at the time: see the IMF’s external sector reports of 2023 and 2024 . I would argue that neglecting the exchange rate was the key reason the IMF’s kept forecasting, incorrectly, that China’s current account surplus would fall (See this blog with Shahin Vallee ). The IMF certainly didn’t warn that China’s property downturn and the RMB’s real depreciation risked a second China shock in its 2022 , 2023 , or 2024 surveillance reports. Concretely, the weaker RMB appears to have contributed to a very large outperformance of China’s exports relative to global trade. See the following chart: That incidentally also happened after the RMB followed the dollar down in 2003. In both periods, there were significant structural shifts. The WTO accession in 2002, and the success of Chinese industrial policies in the “green” industrial sectors and autos in 2022. In both cses exports were turbocharged when structural shifts that should have resulted in a stronger currency were instead amplified by currency weakness. No matter. Paul Krugman has noted that a country that is converging technologically with its trade partners should see a trend appreciation in its currency. China got the technological convergence, but not the real appreciation—at least not until this year. And the move since the middle of 2025 has corrected the depreciation of the RMB that occurred when the RMB followed the dollar down on liberation day, but not the structural overvaluation. Now, there is an argument that exchange rate adjustment is too hot an issue to make it a priority. The PBOC isn’t interested it seems. And some believe that in the interest of comity and good relations with China, the IMF should mirror the PBOC’s views. After all a stronger RMB would slow China’s exports and thus slow China’s economy at a time when China needs export growth to escape deflation and generate employment. Or so the argument goes. Concerns about “external balance“ and the negative global spillovers from China’s rising goods surplus should be ignored and the Fund’s sole focus should be on policies that lead to internal balance. That provides one rationale for the Fund’s ongoing decision to essentially ignore the contentious issue of the PBOC’s ongoing exchange rate management. That argument, however, assumes that China’s economy is small and thus China’s external surplus can safely be ignored because it isn’t a drag on the growth of the IMF’s other members. That clearly isn’t true. And it isn’t clear that China is more interested in having a negotiation over its level of basic pension benefits or the size of its fiscal deficit (where the IMF continues to make timid recommendations that would not move the needle—and certainly wouldn’t meaningfully reduce China’s external surplus) than a discussion over its currency practices. **** Back in the world of fixed but adjustable exchange rates, there was an expectation (not always met to be sure) that surplus countries would allow their currencies to strengthen to bring their economies back into external balance, and that other policy tools would be used to ensure internal balance. I would argue that China’s exchange rate (against both the dollar and the basket) has many similarities to the old world of fixed but adjustable currencies. True, it moves on a controlled path when it moves between different levels rather than jumping up and down. But the PBOC does frequently target a level, and that targeted level does change over time. I would further argue that steps like the recent tariff rate quota that will limit China’s exports of hybrid cars to Europe to around 350,000 units next year (up from 2025, but well below the 800,000 units of 2026) aren’t going to address the underlying imbalance on their own. They can provide a bit of a buffer for specific sectors. But that buffer, while necessary, won’t address the broad-based erosion of manufacturing capacity outside China. This erosion will persist as long as an undervalued RMB sends the entire world a signal to use China as its production base. The new system of managed trade that is emerging in autos would need to be progressively expanded to an ever-increasing set of sectors if protection is used as a substitute for both domestic reform in China and exchange rate adjustment. That is now the direction of travel, but it doesn’t address the underlying systemic issues . Incidentally, those who believe the path of internal demand is critical to rebalancing and that exchange rate moves are secondary need to explain how an acceleration in domestic demand would, on its own, lead China’s external accounts to adjust. One important, stylized fact about China is that domestic demand growth is no longer feeding over to import growth (ex-gold, that is). Bottom line: China, which needs a 1.5 percentage point contribution from net exports every year , is on a collision course with its trading partners without a currency correction that provides the basis for more balanced trade even in the absence of trade restrictions. And there isn’t a realistic path towards balance that doesn’t involve a stronger RMB; there aren’t, as Paul Krugman once put it, immaculate transfers . * That downturn shows up in domestic deflationary pressure, and weak job growth/high rates of (at least youth) unemployment. China, in other words, isn’t in “internal balance.” I really liked the report from Kamakshya Trivedi and Hui Shan of Goldman Sachs arguing China needs two tools to hit two targets (internal and external balance). ** To be sure, rate differentials matter for exporter conversion—but so does the expected movement of the RMB. The market understands this better than the Fund. The Chen and Suwanapruti (Goldman Sachs) note uses a framework similar to mine to describe the CNY’s moves in Q3: “In our view, sizeable FX inflows have continued to support RMB appreciation despite unfavorable interest rate differentials, as strong export receipts and increased exporter FX conversions have outweighed portfolio outflows. Our estimated FX conversion ratio rose to 63% in August, compared with around 45% in normal years, likely reflecting a shift in market expectations from RMB depreciation to appreciation.” *** Šefčovič has jurisdiction over trade policy (narrowly defined), but not broader macroeconomic policies. Europe’s institutional architecture for exchange rate coordination is not well-developed . **** The current account surplus is no longer masked to the same extent as in 2023 and 2024, as SAFE has fiddled with its BoP methodology once again ( per the Federal Reserve ) and the BoP goods surplus is no longer significantly below the customs goods surplus. Of course, there are still problems in the data—the deficit in the investment income account most obviously, but also the recent surge in “customs” gold imports. items.summary_en: The Plaza Accord was not an externally imposed punishment of Japan but part of a broader restructuring that Japanese economists and policymakers themselves recognized was necessary. Its effects were undermined, however, when Tokyo responded to the resulting slowdown with policies that exacerbated investment, credit expansion, and the very imbalances the adjustment was intended to resolve.

Its effects were undermined, however, when Tokyo responded to the resulting slowdown with policies that exacerbated investment, credit expansion, and the very imbalances the adjustment was intended to resolve. Link Copied By Michael Pettis Published on Sep 25, 2026 In recent weeks and months there has been a resurgence in discussions in Europe and the United States about whether or not China should appreciate its currency in response to its enormous trade surpluses. As part of this discussion, analysts often point to the similarities between China today and Japan during the lead-up to the September 1985 Plaza Accord. In response to these discussions, however, Beijing has insisted that China will never tolerate a scenario where China plays the role once played by Japan. Last month, for example, former Chinese ambassador to the United States Cui Tiankai said , “I wish to advise people to give up the illusion that another Plaza Accord could be imposed on China. They should give up the illusion that China will ever give in to intimidation, coercion or groundless accusation.” Unfortunately, much of the discussion, including China’s response, is based on a very confused and highly politicized understanding of Japan’s economic performance in the 1990s and 2000s. The conventional account of the Plaza Accord—especially among China analysts—is that the United States forced Japan to accept a sharp appreciation of the yen, destroying Japanese export competitiveness, causing its economy to collapse, and eventually producing the Japanese “lost decades.” In this view, forcing a change in the value of the yen was a violation of Japanese sovereignty aimed at forcing Japan to give up its economic leadership. There are two problems with this interpretation. The first obvious problem is that for years Japan, along with Germany and other countries, had participated in exchange-rate policies and interventions that boosted the dollar’s value against their own currencies, contributing to a prolonged appreciation in the real value of the U.S. dollar that made American manufacturers far less competitive than their Japanese and European counterparts. The fact that Japanese intervention in the value of the U.S. dollar was not generally considered in Japan to be a violation of U.S. sovereignty, even as it undermined U.S. manufacturing, suggests that similar intervention from the other side should not have been considered a violation of Japanese sovereignty so much as a normal consequence of participation in the global trading system. A currency exchange rate, after all, does not belong to one country, but rather to that country and all of its trading partners. If the right to manipulate foreign currencies is symmetrical, this of course creates a parallel between Japan in the 1980s and China today, with the latter having actively intervened in the value of the U.S. dollar for decades, in ways that benefit its manufacturers while undermining those of the United States. Second, and more importantly, the problem with the conventional account of the Plaza Accord is that it gets the economic mechanism wrong. The Plaza Accord did not cause Japan’s long stagnation. Its purpose was to force an adjustment in the then-uneven distribution of global demand so that the manufacturing sectors of countries like Germany and Japan were no longer able to benefit from many years of weak domestic demand and wage suppression at the expense of their trade partners. By the mid-1980s, many Japanese and European policymakers recognized that the existing imbalances were unsustainable, but found it very difficult to reverse them. According to Japan’s own analysis, for example, the Japanese economy needed to transfer a greater share of total income to the household sector. This was most obvious from the famous report in 1986 by the Maekawa Commission, set up by former prime minister Nakasone Yasuhiro precisely to determine how Japan should respond to the international imbalances that had emerged. Resolving Japan’s Consumption Imbalance The report did not treat yen appreciation as an external punishment that Japan needed to resist. On the contrary, it argued that Japan had reached a point at which its postwar growth model had to be fundamentally changed. Japan’s current-account surplus had reached 3.6 percent of GNP in 1985, and the Maekawa Commission argued that the resulting external imbalance had reached a critical phase for Japan as well as for the international economy. Japan, it argued , needed a “historic” transformation away from an economy dependent on external demand and toward one led by domestic demand . The commission—and a growing number of Japanese economists and economic policy advisors—therefore called for a fundamental restructuring of Japan’s trade and industrial structure, greater imports and market access, more domestic consumption, better housing and urban development, reduced working hours, and higher disposable income. It also called for reducing the incentives that encouraged excessive household saving. The objective was to change the composition of Japanese demand and production. Among other things, this meant reducing Japan’s overreliance on trade surpluses and domestic investment—both of which at the time had become excessively high—to balance weak domestic consumption. A stronger yen was a part of that transition. It would reduce the purchasing-price advantage enjoyed by Japanese exporters while increasing the real purchasing power of Japanese households. Imports would become cheaper, Japanese consumers would be able to consume more for the same nominal income, thus increasing the share they retained of total GDP, and resources could gradually move out of industries whose competitiveness depended on suppressed domestic wages and an undervalued currency. The same logic applied to Germany. In both countries, domestic demand was too weak relative to productive capacity, so excess production was exported in the form of current-account surpluses. The adjustment therefore needed to be broadly symmetric: surplus countries would rely less on exports and more on domestic demand, while deficit countries would rely less on domestic demand and more on production for export. More appropriately valued currencies were part of this adjustment, but they were assumed to be only part of a deeper restructuring to change the distribution of income and the composition of demand. The initial consequences were not necessarily evidence of a policy failure. The yen appreciated sharply, Japanese exports became less competitive, imports became cheaper, and the real purchasing power of Japanese households increased. But because domestic consumption did not rise sufficiently quickly to replace lost external demand, Japanese production and GDP growth slowed. IMF estimates show that export volumes contracted by about 6 percent in 1986, while GDP growth fell from roughly 5 percent in 1985 to 2.5 percent in 1986. That slowdown may have shocked Tokyo, but it should have been obvious that without a sudden surge in consumption—something that was always unlikely—a slowdown was a necessary part of the longer-term adjustment. If an economy needs to shift demand from exports and investment toward household consumption, and consumption does not immediately accelerate enough to offset the loss of external demand, the adjustment must initially appear as slower growth. Contradictory Policy Implementation The critical mistake was what happened next. Rather than allowing the appreciation of the yen to work through the economy and facilitate the necessary shift toward household consumption and other forms of domestic demand, Japanese policymakers attempted to offset the slowdown with exceptionally easy monetary policy. Interest rates were cut sharply, and credit expanded rapidly. The intention, perhaps understandably, was to prevent the appreciation of the yen from causing a recession. But the extent of the response, perhaps reflecting the authorities’ concern over the immediate slowdown, was almost certainly excessive. The Bank of Japan’s (BoJ) official discount rate was 5 percent when the Plaza Accord was signed in September 1985. It was then cut five times between January 1986 and February 1987, to 2.5 percent, where it remained for more than two years before the BoJ began tightening in May 1989. The result was that in the end Tokyo, contrary to the recommendation of its economists and hoping to adjust without adjustment costs, took steps to prevent the stronger yen from raising household incomes and consumption. By expanding credit and making borrowing so much cheaper, Tokyo largely reversed the income-distribution impact of the currency appreciation. A currency appreciation rebalances weak consumption by effectively shifting purchasing power from net exporters toward net importers. Because Japanese households were overwhelmingly net importers, while the manufacturing sector included overwhelmingly net exporters, the appreciation should have shifted purchasing power from manufacturers toward households, raising the very low household share of Japanese GDP, just as the Maekawa Commission report recommended. But by lowering interest rates and expanding credit, Tokyo reversed much of this positive impact. In a system like Japan’s in the 1980s, the banking system overwhelmingly borrowed from households and lent to businesses and government. Lowering interest rates therefore effectively transferred income from households, which were net creditors, back to businesses and government, which were net borrowers, reversing the direction of the previous transfer. The stronger yen was supposed to raise real household income and the consumption share of GDP, while lower interest rates reversed the impact of reduced household interest income and increased the resources available to borrowers. Financial repression therefore substantially offset the distributional effect through which currency appreciation was supposed to promote domestic rebalancing. Nor did the impact stop with the distribution of income. Tokyo’s monetary easing in reaction to the Plaza Accord encouraged banks to expand lending aggressively, particularly into property and other asset markets. Asset prices soared, collateral values increased, credit standards weakened, and the resulting rise in apparent wealth encouraged still more borrowing. The Plaza Accord thus interacted with a financial system already predisposed toward excessive investment. Easy credit did not simply offset the short-term contraction in external demand; it redirected the adjustment toward debt-financed investment and asset-price inflation. Rather than reducing Japan’s dependence on excessive investment, the credit boom temporarily masked the need for structural rebalancing and produced even more nonproductive property, infrastructure, and manufacturing capacity. The Cause of the “Lost Decades” This is why it is misleading to say that the Plaza Accord “caused” Japan’s lost decades. Many years of a severely unbalanced economy created the need for adjustment, but Tokyo was unwilling to bear the short-term adjustment costs. As a result, the Bank of Japan kept policy exceptionally loose during 1987–1989, with one IMF analysis estimating that the policy rate was roughly four percentage points below what a conventional policy rule would have expected during this period. The result was an extraordinary expansion of lending into preexisting rising asset prices and increasingly excessive investment in infrastructure and technology-driven manufacturing capacity. Even before the credit expansion, Japan’s dominance of global manufacturing, especially in advanced technology production, and its world-famous infrastructure suggested that investment may already have exceeded what could be economically justified. After the credit expansion, Japan’s dominance of advanced-technology manufacturing accelerated further, as did infrastructure spending, including projects subsequently described as “bridges to nowhere,” while the credit boom helped unleash what by many measures was the greatest property bubble in history. Once the bubble burst, Japan faced a much larger problem than the original loss of export competitiveness. Land prices fell dramatically, equity prices collapsed, and banks were left with enormous quantities of loans secured by assets worth far less than when the loans were made. Nonperforming loans surged, bank capital deteriorated, and banks became much more reluctant to lend. But even the banking crisis does not fully explain the subsequent stagnation. The deeper problem was the enormous stock of excess capital accumulated during the preceding years. Japan had invested too much in property, infrastructure, manufacturing capacity, and other forms of capital whose economic returns were far below what had been assumed when the investment was made. The bubble made this problem worse by making those investments appear more valuable than they were. When asset prices collapsed, the excess became visible. The Japanese economy did not simply need more demand. It needed instead to unwind a capital stock that had become too large relative to profitable investment opportunities. The IMF has explicitly described the prolonged weakness of Japanese investment in terms of the need to unwind the excess capital inherited from the years of overinvestment. Gross fixed capital formation rose from about 30 percent of GDP before the Plaza Accord to 34–35 percent by 1990, before falling to less than 29 percent by the end of the 1990s and to about 26 percent by 2005. This distinction matters because a decline in investment is not always evidence of a demand problem that can be solved with more stimulus. When an economy has spent years increasing investment faster than its productive opportunities, a subsequent decline in investment can be part of the necessary adjustment. Japan’s problem was not that Japanese workers had suddenly become unproductive or that Japanese manufacturers had suddenly lost all international competitiveness; it was that too much of the economy had been built around investment that no longer made economic sense. The lesson of Japan, then, is not that the Plaza Accord destroyed the Japanese economy. Germany, after all, underwent the same currency adjustment at roughly the same time, but because it had not engaged in nearly the same extent of misallocated investment as Japan—either before the Plaza Accord or, more importantly, after—it did not experience an equivalent surge in debt or the same economic consequences. The general lesson is that an economy with a large external surplus eventually has to rebalance, and how that rebalancing is managed matters enormously. Japan’s own analysts had identified much of what needed to be done before the bubble and stagnation occurred. They argued that Japan needed to allow households to capture more of the benefits of the stronger yen, increase consumption, reduce dependence on investment and external demand, and allow resources to move away from sectors with excess capacity. But instead of using currency appreciation to play a role in this needed adjustment, Tokyo used exceptionally easy credit to preserve the old growth model. The Plaza Accord therefore did not turn a healthy Japanese economy into an unhealthy one. It exposed an underlying imbalance that had to be addressed and that wasn’t. Japan’s mistake was to respond to the resulting slowdown not by completing the shift toward domestic demand and accepting the short-term adjustment costs, but by using debt-financed investment to postpone the adjustment and accelerate the problem of unproductive investment. The resulting bubble did not eliminate the underlying imbalance but converted what should have been the beginning of an external adjustment into a domestic investment and financial crisis. The Lesson for China This is where the Plaza Accord becomes particularly relevant to China. China should not look at Japan’s experience and conclude that currency appreciation is inherently dangerous, or that reducing its trade surplus will inevitably produce a Japanese-style collapse. The real lesson is almost the opposite. China’s current growth model—based on high exports, weak consumption, and excessive investment—is ultimately unsustainable. Beijing cannot choose whether China will adjust; one way or another, it will. What it can choose is how painful that adjustment will be. If China needs to reduce an excessive external surplus, the objective should be to increase domestic demand and reduce the economy’s dependence on investment and external demand. Currency appreciation can be part of that process, but of course it cannot be the whole process. The greater danger is responding to weaker exports with another round of credit-financed investment. China has done this before, most notably after the global financial crisis of 2008–2009, which caused a sharp contraction in its trade surplus, and in retrospect, marked the beginning of the current period of unbalanced growth. That is precisely what Japan did after 1985, and China is even more vulnerable because it has a much larger stock of potential excess investment to unwind in property, infrastructure, and manufacturing capacity. If weaker external demand is met by encouraging more borrowing and domestic investment, regardless of whether that investment is economically justified, China risks postponing the inevitable. China therefore faces the same basic choice Japan confronted, but with deeper imbalances and less accommodating global conditions. It can shift a larger share of national income toward households and allow consumption to absorb more of what the economy produces; or it can continue relying on investment, despite increasingly weak returns; or it can allow production and growth to slow. The first choice requires a substantial change in the domestic distribution of income and the incentives to save. The second risks still more debt and excess capacity and, ultimately, a more painful adjustment. The third implies higher unemployment and weaker growth. That is the real lesson of Japan and the Plaza Accord. The problem was never that Japan was forced to give up an economic model that had once been extraordinarily successful. It was that the model had become increasingly incompatible with Japan’s level of development, and the subsequent policy response preserved too much of it for too long. China faces a similar challenge today. The issue is not whether it will rebalance, but whether it will do so by shifting income and demand toward households, or by postponing the adjustment for a few more years through further accumulation of debt and excess capacity. items.summary_en: The world isn’t moving away from the dollar. It is shifting its dollars from traditional reserves to state banks, pension funds, and other quasi-sovereign investors.
items.body: Council on Foreign Relations By experts and staff Published September 15, 2026 8:37 a.m. Brad W. Setser CFR Expert Whitney Shepardson Senior Fellow This is a joint blog with Alex Etra , Senior Macro Strategist and head of Flow of Funds at Vanda Research . The IMF’s data on the currency composition of foreign exchange (FX) reserves is scrutinized carefully for any signs that the world is shifting way from the dollar. Yet it doesn’t really matter that much if the dollar’s share of reserves has shifted from 56.5 percent to 57 percent. The ink-to-impact ratio of the quarterly reporting on the latest COFER data is all off. Neither the stock of global reserves nor the stock of dollar reserves has changed much in the last ten years. The action is elsewhere. China’s state banks (per the Bank of International Settlements) have almost as many foreign assets as the central bank (PBOC). Japan’s Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF) has almost as many foreign assets ( $986 billion ) as the government has FX reserves ($1.1 trillion at the end of August). Japan’s FX reserves are on the books of the Ministry of Finance and the GPIF is overseen by the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Labor—so these are almost all assets of the Government of Japan or the broader public sector, not its central bank. Korea’s National Pension Service has more foreign assets than the Bank of Korea has FX reserves. A different dynamic is in play in Taiwan, as the government doesn’t run a big retirement fund. But in a world where the hedge ratio of the life insurers has been (and still is) used as a policy tool, the shift in Taiwan’s foreign asset accumulation away from the Central Bank of China (CBC) and over to institutions whose activities in the foreign currency market it directly influences broadly fits into the same theme. So too does the PBOC’s use of the “macroprudential adjustment factor” effectively adjust banks’ net foreign assets in much the same way that CBC regulations adjust lifer hedge ratios. In the last year, the lifers’ hedge ratios—and their direct hedges with the central bank—have been one of the key tools the CBC has used to manage the Taiwan dollar (and guard the lifers’ solvency). Asia’s big surplus economies are in a sense just catching up with the world’s oil exporters. Norway put its oil surplus into a sovereign wealth fund from the start. Kuwait, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi (the most oil-rich emirate) all also have large sovereign funds. And the world’s biggest oil exporter has joined them: The Public Investment Fund has almost as many foreign assets as the Saudi Central Bank (SAMA).* What’s more, the available evidence suggests that the dollar share of these pools is in line with or higher than the dollar share of global FX reserves (it depends on the institution and jurisdiction). In other words, by looking at the (easily available) data on the world’s static holdings of formal FX reserve assets, scholars and analysts miss most of the growth in the world’s sovereign and quasi-sovereign foreign assets. Consider China. No serious analyst now disputes that China’s state banks—including the policy banks (the China Development Bank, China Exim)—hold several trillion in foreign assets . China reports $3.3 trillion in gross foreign assets to the BIS (the net position, counting foreign bank claims on the entire Chinese economy not just the banks, is $2.5 trillion). That maps to the BOP data, which shows almost $4 trillion in gross outflows through the banking system (technically, the sum of gross outflows in “other” plus the $500 billion in foreign currency bonds held by the state commercial banks) Since 2010 (and even more so after 2014) the net outflow through the state banks has exceeded reserve accumulation. The broad contours of this story are confirmed by the balance sheet data reported by state commercial banks in their 2025 annual reports, which showed that the top five banks held a combined $2.5 trillion in foreign currency assets (mostly held abroad). The Chinese haven’t disclosed the foreign assets of the two policy banks (with at this stage the complicity of the IMF, which has neither analyzed the role of SAFE policy bank financing, nor highlighted the glaring gap in China’s own reporting). But the work of AidData points to nearly $1 trillion in foreign assets, with a hefty dollar share. The available data sources all suggest that the bulk of the foreign assets of the state banks are in dollars. SAFE’s disclosure—which covers the commercial banks—puts the dollar share of their offshore foreign currency assets at around 70 percent. That is well above the last disclosed dollar share of China’s formal reserves (55 percent in 2019). The banks’ annual reports suggest that about 70 percent of the banks’ assets are in dollars and Hong Kong dollars (55 percent USD/15 percent HKD)—a bit below the dollar and Hong Kong dollar share of their liabilities (swaps out of the HKD fund a decent share of the banks euro assets). Put simply, SAFE’s static dollar holdings aren’t the important story. The real story is the rapid growth of the state banks dollar holdings . Japan holds a high (though undisclosed) dollar share in its FX reserves, and those reserves are primarily invested in Treasuries—so Japan’s MoF is now clearly the largest contributor to the U.S. data on foreign official holdings of Treasuries. ( SAFE has shifted its funds out of U.S. custodians , and thus increasingly appears in the data as a “private” holder in a European custodial center) Japan’s formal reserves haven’t changed much in the last ten years; periodic sales to limit the yen’s weakness have offset most of the MoF’s accumulated interest income. Foreign currency reserves were $1.2 trillion in 2014 and $1.16 trillion at the end of Q1. They dipped to about $1 trillion at the end of August after sales of close to $100 billion at the end of July/start of August. What has grown is the foreign portfolio of the GPIF. it was around $400 billion in 2014, ~$1 trillion in Q1 of 2026. GPIF’s foreign bonds aren’t held exclusively in dollars, but roughly 52 percent of its foreign bonds (26 percent of all bonds) are USD-denominated. But the GPIF, like most international investors, holds a large share of its equity portfolio in the U.S. (~$165 billion, 65 percent of the foreign equity portfolio). Korea is a more extreme version of Japan. The Bank of Korea’s FX reserves have been roughly $375-450 billion over the last ten years or so. Around two-thirds of those are now in dollars (as of the end of 2025). From 2012 to 2025, the foreign assets at the NPS have grown from ~$80 billion (around 21 percent of total assets) to over $660 billion (55 percent of total assets)—and something like 70 percent of those are in dollars. 76 percent of the fund’s equities are in dollars, and 66 percent of its debt. And while a lower share of its “alternative” portfolio is in North America, most alternative mandates are awarded in dollars. In other words, the majority of the dollar assets held by Korea’s government (the NPS reports to the Ministry of Health and Welfare, and the Minister of Health chairs its asset allocation committee) aren’t held by the central bank and aren’t in the IMF’s COFER data set. Taiwan is an unusual case, as the life insurers aren’t technically sovereign investors. But with their regulator now explicitly encouraging the them to hold an unhedged foreign currency book and hence they now rely on the state for their solvency, they have a bit of an official character (a significant appreciation of the TWD would blow through their volatility reserves and leave them with fewer assets than liabilities, as their foreign assets are largely held against TWD policies). The CBC certainly now uses the lifers desire to unwind existing hedges to help manage the Taiwan dollar. And they have an exceptionally high dollar share in their foreign assets—over 95 percent. The Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF) is another example. It keeps roughly $200 billion of its $250 billion in foreign investments in dollars—well above the U.S. share of a standard global stock index. Almost all of the PIF’s $30 billion in external debt is also in dollars. And the PIF now has only slightly fewer foreign assets than the Saudi Central Bank has reserves.** The broad story is thus pretty clear: the growth in the world’s sovereign and quasi-sovereign assets is not coming through an increase in FX reserve holdings managed by the world’s central banks. And, in the critical case of China, the dollar share of China’s quasi-sovereign foreign assets is likely higher than the dollar share of their formal FX reserves. Adam Tooze has noted that inflows into the U.S. are now coming from investors looking for a profit, not investors looking for safety. What he calls the “profit dollar” manifests itself in a number of different ways. More inflows into corporate bonds and equities for one. Less official demand for Treasuries for another. More opacity too. Those same trends are at play among sovereign and quasi-sovereign investors. So don’t obsess about the dollar’s chare in formal FX reserves. Do recognize that the dollar’s “reserve currency role” isn’t the source of any significant new inflows into the dollar. The dollar’s dominant role in the international monetary system depends on much more than the size and composition of central bank FX reserves. It is as much, perhaps more so (given that FX reserve managers are themselves ultimately liability matchers) a function of the portfolio choice of a set of private/semi-private/quasi-sovereign investors that are much more difficult to observe. Reserve currency status is not only about FX reserves in a strict sense. That’s been true for some time. Most of the current flow into U.S. from the “official” sector is coming from investors who are not classic reserve managers. Those flows remain heavily tilted toward the dollar, at least for now.*** And any real de-dollarization would likely occur first among these investors. Put differently, the dollar’s global role is increasingly as a source of returns, not a source of safety. The foreign bid, private and public, is for risk, not for Treasuries. That doesn’t help Scott Bessent much right now, but it has helped keep valuations in the stock market extended. And the global debate on the dollar’s role lags the evolution in the dollar’s role, and the risks associated with that new role. It is currently fashionable in some circles to point to the diminution of the “convenience yield” on Treasuries even while the U.S. dollar continues to enjoy such a privilege. But the shift in the global investor base, and their apparent portfolio preference for U.S. risk assets in lieu of Treasuries, may help explain the divergence between the convenience yield on UST and the convenience yield on USD. And of course, if the negative convenience yield implies that Treasuries are trading at a historical discount, the persistence of the latter—and its concentration in risk assets—suggests that the “profit dollar” itself is likely trading at a historical premium. That apparent premium on U.S. risk assets deserves as much (or more) scrutiny as the currency composition of central bank FX reserves. * The PIF and Saudi Aramco also now have a certain amount of debt. ** Reserves (now mostly in Treasuries, so should appear in the TIC data, unlike at some times in the past. *** Japan is the main exception; the GPIF’s dollar share is below the likely dollar share of Japan’s MoF.
